fix_commit.message: Fix incorrect buffer size computation for the base64() extension function. [forum:/forumpost/b1993c858f|Forum post b1993c858f].
fix_commit.author: drh

findings.title: Incorrect operator precedence in base64() buffer-size calculation causes undersized allocation and heap overflow
findings.message: In the base64(x) UDF, the number of base64 'quads' required to encode a blob of nv bytes is computed with the expression `nc = 4*(nv+2/3);`. Because the C `/` operator binds tighter than `+`, this is parsed as `4*(nv + (2/3))` = `4*(nv + 0)` = `4*nv`, instead of the intended `4*((nv+2)/3)` (ceil(nv/3) quads). The computed `nc` is roughly 4/3 smaller than the real requirement. `nc` (declared as `int`) is then used both to size the `sqlite3_malloc(nc)` allocation and to drive the subsequent encoding loop that writes `nc` bytes into `cBuf`. For large blobs (e.g. ~1.1 GB, close to SQLITE_MAX_LENGTH), the undersized buffer combined with the encode loop's actual byte production leads to a heap-based buffer overflow; in extreme cases involving very large nv the arithmetic used elsewhere to size/check the buffer can also signed-integer-overflow. This is exploitable any time an attacker can control the size of a blob/string passed to base64().
findings.suggestion: Add explicit parentheses so integer division is applied to the total byte count before multiplying by 4, e.g. `nc = 4*((nv+2)/3);`. Additionally, widen `nc` to a 64-bit type (e.g. `sqlite3_int64`) before performing arithmetic that scales with `nv`, since `nv` itself can approach INT_MAX and `4*nv` can overflow a 32-bit `int` even when the division is fixed.

ground_truth.root_cause: Missing parentheses around `nv+2` before the division by 3 in the buffer-size formula `4*(nv+2/3)` causes C operator-precedence rules (division binds tighter than addition) to compute the wrong quad count, producing an undersized allocation.

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Incorrect operator precedence in base64() buffer-size calculation causes undersized allocation and heap overflow
